tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Documentation

Taskflow keeps three kinds of document under `docs/`. They do not carry equal weight.

| Folder | What it is | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| `docs/adr/` | Architecture Decision Records: numbered, dated, reviewed. | **Authoritative.** |
| `docs/product/` | Product notes written before or alongside a feature: intent, examples, wording. | Context only. |
| `docs/support/` | Runbooks and support macros: what people observed. | Describes behaviour, never specifies it. |

## Precedence

1. An ADR is the specification for every question it addresses. The highest-numbered ADR that addresses a question is the one that applies; a later ADR supersedes an earlier one only where it says so.
2. Where a product note and an ADR disagree, the ADR wins. A product note that predates an ADR on the same subject is kept for history, not as a second opinion.
3. Support notes record what was seen at the time. They are never evidence of intended behaviour.
4. Code comments, `TODO`s and function names are not documentation. They are frequently stale.
5. Where no document speaks, the current behaviour of the code is authoritative, and a new feature follows the conventions of its sibling features (same error classes, same guards, same events).
# ADR 0009 — The issue list filter vocabulary

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-03-02
- Supersedes: the "Filters" section of `docs/product/issue-list-notes.md` where the two disagree.

## Context

The issue list is filtered from the URL: the filter bar writes query parameters, the page reads
them back, the Server Action and the export tooling send the same shape to the service, and the
repository turns it into predicates. Three copies of "what does `status=…` mean" have grown
apart. This record fixes one vocabulary and names the places that must agree on it.

## Decision

1. **One vocabulary, three places.** The URL codec (`parseIssueFilterParams` /
   `issueFilterToParams`), the filter schema that validates every server entry point, and the
   repository predicates accept the same values and give them the same meaning. A value the
   codec produces is a value the schema accepts and the repository understands. Pages do not
   parse the query string themselves.

2. **`assignee` / `author`.** A user id; for `assignee` also `none` (unassigned); for both also
   `me`, the signed-in user. `me` travels unchanged through the codec and the schema and is
   resolved by the service against the acting user, so an API caller and a page get the same
   answer. Omitting the parameter means "do not filter on it".

3. **`status`.** A comma list of statuses and/or the groups `open` and `closed`. `open` stands
   for every status that is not closed; `closed` for the closed statuses (the ones the project
   card and the digest already count as closed). A group expands to its members wherever it is
   read: the codec expands it when parsing, and the schema and the repository accept the group
   names as well, so `status=open` means the same on a page and in an API call. Unknown values
   are dropped by the codec and refused by the schema.

4. **`label`.** A comma list of label ids. An issue matches only when it carries **every** listed
   label (all-of). Any-of is what the status and priority lists do; labels are different because
   people narrow with them ("bug" and "regression"), they do not widen.

5. **`due_before`.** Either a calendar date `YYYY-MM-DD` or a full ISO-8601 timestamp.
   - A calendar date is read in UTC and matches issues due at any time on that day **or
     earlier** — the whole day is included.
   - A full timestamp matches issues due strictly before that instant, as it always has.
   Issues without a due date never match.

6. **`archived`.** `1` includes archived issues alongside live ones; `only` lists archived issues
   and nothing else. Absent, the list shows live issues only.

7. **`priority`** is a comma list (any-of); **`q`** is a substring of the title or description;
   **`project`** narrows to one project. Unchanged.

8. **The reported `total` counts exactly the issues the filter matches**, at every entry point.

## Consequences

- The "Assigned to me" sidebar link (`issues?assignee=me`) is a real filter, not a convention.
- The "My issues" page's hard-coded list of open statuses becomes `status=open`.
# Issue list — product notes

_Written for the filter bar launch (2025-12). Kept for history; see `docs/adr/0009-issue-list-filters.md` for the current rules._

## Filters

The filter bar narrows the issue list and writes what it did into the URL, so a filtered list is
a link you can send to a colleague.

- **Status** — chips for the six statuses; several chips show issues in any of them.
- **Assignee** — a member, or "Unassigned". The sidebar's "Assigned to me" entry just links to the
  list with the current user's id filled in.
- **Labels** — pick several and the list shows issues that have any of them, exactly like status.
- **Due before** — a timestamp; issues due at that instant or later are left out. The date picker
  sends midnight of the chosen day, so the chosen day itself is not shown.
- **Show archived** — a toggle that mixes archived issues into the list. There is no archived-only
  view; people who need one use the export.

The project page and the "My issues" page read the URL themselves; "My issues" shows the open
statuses unless the URL names statuses.

## Counts

The header count ("12 issues in Platform") is the number of rows the filter matches.

## Precedence

1. An ADR is the specification for every question it addresses. The highest-numbered ADR that addresses a question is the one that applies; a later ADR supersedes an earlier one only where it says so.

content.text:
I've fixed all six reports. The URL parsing, the request validation and the listing now follow the filter rules in `docs/adr/0009-issue-list-filters.md`, and the total shown with a page counts exactly the rows the filter matches. The existing suite still passes (617 tests) and typecheck and lint are clean. I also ran a throwaway test from /tmp, since deleted, that took each report's URL through to the database query. Every case returned the right issues and the right total.

1. **"Assigned to me" empty list:** the sidebar link was broken: its `?` got percent-encoded, so it pointed to a page that doesn't exist. It now goes to `/<org>/issues?assignee=me`. `me` (also for `author`) passes through unchanged and is swapped for the signed-in user only when the list is fetched, so a page and an API call get the same answer.
2. **"Unassigned" shows everything:** `assignee=none` now returns only issues nobody is assigned to. Before, "unassigned" was treated the same as "no assignee filter".
3. **Two labels:** an issue must now carry every listed label. The rows and the header count use the same query, so they agree.
4. **Due before:**
   - A plain date like `2026-03-02` is now accepted and includes that whole day (UTC).
   - A full timestamp still means "strictly before that moment", and timestamps with a UTC offset are now accepted too.
   - Issues with no due date never match.
5. **`status=open`:** `open` (every status that isn't done or canceled) and `closed` (done and canceled) are now accepted everywhere. The export route now applies the list filters, and the filter bar has Open and Closed chips.
6. **Archived:** `archived=only` lists archived issues and nothing else; `archived=1` still adds them to the live list. The filter bar has a matching control.

The project issue list, the "My issues" page and the export now read the URL through the same parsing code instead of doing it themselves. I also added a "Me" option to the filter bar's assignee menu.

Decision for you: "My issues" still shows your own open issues when the URL doesn't name an assignee or a status. The ADR only asks for the open-status default, and I kept the assignee default to match how the page behaves today. The catch is that the dashboard's "All issues" link and the sidebar's "Issues" link land on that same page, so they show only your issues. Making it a true all-issues list when no assignee is given means dropping that default. I didn't, because it changes what the page shows.

The main changes are in `src/hooks/issue-filter-params.ts`, `src/schemas/issue.ts`, `src/server/repositories/issue-repository.ts` and `src/server/services/issue-service.ts`.
